Instead of a single processor tackling tasks one after another, multiple processors work together at the same time. This approach is essential today because the demand for faster data processing has outgrown the speed limits of single-core processors. The primary goals of parallel computing are to increase speed, improve efficiency, and handle larger datasets. By splitting workloads, systems can complete tasks in a fraction of the time compared to sequential processing. Furthermore, parallel computing allows us to solve problems that are too large for a single machine, such as modeling global weather patterns or simulating molecular structures for drug discovery. It also enhances reliability; if one processor fails in a cluster, others can often take over the work, ensuring the system keeps running.

Applications of parallel computing are everywhere in modern life. Scientists use supercomputers to simulate nuclear explosions or understand the formation of galaxies. The advantages of this technology are clear: it offers significantly higher throughput, better resource utilization, and the ability to scale up as needs grow. However, there are limitations. Programming for parallel systems is difficult; developers must carefully manage how data moves between processors to avoid errors.
